paragraphs.text: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-89 (DEE89) is an autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder. Seizures begin in the first months of life and are mainly epileptic spasms, myoclonic seizures, or focal motor seizures, often with a suppression-burst EEG pattern. Affected individuals have severe developmental delay and abnormal muscle tone. Some also have non-neural features, including cleft palate, omphalocele, talipes equinovarus, joint contractures, skeletal abnormalities, and dysmorphic features (Chatron et al., 2020; Neuray et al., 2020).

checks.claim: DEE89 is an autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: Sanger sequencing confirmed segregation of the GAD1 variants with the disease phenotype (Supplementary Fig. 1) and a recessive mode of inheritance associated with the disease.

paragraphs.text: Chatron et al. (2020) reported 11 patients from 6 consanguineous families with a neonatal-onset syndromic developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. In all 11 patients, seizures began in the first 2 months of life, mainly as epileptic spasms or myoclonic seizures. Seven of the 8 patients who had neonatal EEGs showed a suppression-burst or burst attenuation pattern, and the 2 patients first recorded later showed hypsarrhythmia. The authors described increased muscle tone as a core feature, often together with axial hypotonia.

paragraphs.text: In family A of Chatron et al. (2020), the 2 affected children were born to healthy Algerian first-cousin parents. The older child, a boy, presented to the neuropediatric unit at 5 months of age with developmental regression and loss of visual contact, opisthotonus, and axial hypotonia. He had a cleft soft palate, epileptic spasms, and hypsarrhythmia. At 6 years of age he could not sit unassisted, had spastic tetraparesis with limited extension of the knees and elbows, and had no verbal communication. He also had scoliosis and profound intellectual disability. His brain MRI was normal. His sister also had a cleft soft palate. At 2 days of age she was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit with episodes of eye revulsion, cyanosis, and spasm-like movements, and her EEG showed a suppression-burst pattern. At 26 months of age she had severe developmental delay, axial hypotonia, no head control, segmental hypertonia with limited extension of the knees, no visual contact with abnormal eye movements, and no verbal communication.

paragraphs.text: Family B of Chatron et al. (2020) was a consanguineous Egyptian family with 2 affected sibs. In the girl, prenatal scanning showed an omphalocele containing liver, intestinal atresia, and right talipes equinovarus, and there was polyhydramnios. At birth she had an omphalocele and a cleft soft palate. Seizures began at 2 weeks of age as eye twitches and epileptic spasms. Her EEG showed a suppression-burst pattern that evolved to hypsarrhythmia. She had severe developmental delay and spasticity. Brain imaging showed a hypoplastic corpus callosum, cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, and enlarged lateral ventricles. Her dysmorphic features included hypertelorism, downslanting palpebral fissures, microretrognathia, low-set abnormally shaped ears, and neck webbing. She also had multiple skin hemangiomas, limited range of movement in all joints, camptodactyly, rocker-bottom feet, scoliosis, and a large clitoris with hypoplastic labia. She died at 2 years of age from failure to thrive and respiratory infection. Her similarly affected brother had an omphalocele and bilateral talipes equinovarus at birth. He also had arthrogryposis, failure to thrive, global developmental delay, and dysmorphic features similar to his sister's, but no cleft palate. His seizures also began at 2 weeks of age as eye twitches and epileptic spasms. He died at 4 years of age from pulmonary infection and severe growth retardation.

paragraphs.text: Family C of Chatron et al. (2020) was a Turkish family with first-cousin parents. The proband, a 12-year-old girl, developed eyelid myoclonia at 2 weeks of age, followed 1 week later by myoclonic seizures of the upper limbs. She went on to have generalized tonic-clonic seizures and refractory epilepsy. Her EEG showed a suppression-burst pattern and photosensitivity. She had profound intellectual disability, no speech, generalized hypotonia in infancy, and tetraparesis with increased muscle tone. She also had a cleft palate, left-sided talipes, conductive hearing loss, and recurrent episodes of fever without signs of infection. Her brain MRI was normal. Her brother had a similar phenotype, with refractory myoclonic, tonic, and tonic-clonic seizures from the first day of life, a suppression-burst EEG, and a cleft palate. His seizures worsened on a ketogenic diet, and he died from refractory seizures at 2 years of age. At that time he had profound intellectual disability and tetraparesis with increased muscle tone.

paragraphs.text: Family D of Chatron et al. (2020) was an Iranian family with second-cousin parents and a family history of epilepsy and developmental delay. In the male proband, myoclonic seizures were noted within 1 day of birth and later evolved into epileptic spasms; his EEG showed dysrhythmia. He had profound developmental delay and was unable to walk. Imaging showed prominent inner liquor spaces. He initially had reduced muscle tone and later developed spasticity, dystonia, and scoliosis. He had low-set ears, a broad nasal bridge, mild hypertelorism, and a thin upper lip. His sister had epileptic spasms and myoclonic seizures from 7 days of age. Her EEG initially showed burst attenuation and later scattered sharp waves. At 15 months of age she could roll onto her side but could not sit unsupported, and her head circumference was 44 cm (1.2 cm below the 3rd centile). She also had axial hypotonia and mild dystonia. The authors considered a cervical notch seen on her brain MRI to be probably unrelated to GAD1.

paragraphs.text: Family E of Chatron et al. (2020) was a consanguineous Turkish family. At 2 months of age the male proband was referred for facial dysmorphism, developmental delay, cleft palate, Hirschsprung disease, and pes equinovarus. Epileptic spasms were seen on examination and had in retrospect been present since 1 month of age; his EEG showed hypsarrhythmia. His other features included flexion contractures of the elbows and knees, upslanting palpebral fissures, hypertelorism, microretrognathia, low-set ears, cervical and axillary webbing, sparse hair and eyebrows, umbilical hernia, hepatomegaly, hydrocephalus detected in utero, and an atlantoaxial anomaly. On eye examination he had nystagmus, alternating esotropia, and bilateral pale optic discs. His audiogram was normal at birth, but he failed a hearing test at 1 year of age. He also had recurrent aspiration pneumonia, an atrial septal defect, nephrocalcinosis, no head control or eye contact, axial hypotonia, and limb spasticity. His older brother was born at 29 weeks' gestation. He had cleft palate, short neck, narrow thorax, myoclonic seizures, and congenital heart disease (a large patent ductus arteriosus, a small atrial septal defect, and moderate pulmonary hypertension). He also had abdominal distension and pes equinovarus, and he died of sepsis on postnatal day 9.

Three of the 6 patients became seizure-free, yet all had severe intellectual disability, and the authors suggested that GAD1 defects affect development and cognition independently of seizure control.

Seizure onset was at 6 months of age, with bilateral tonic-clonic seizures, refractory epilepsy, and generalized epileptogenic EEG activity. She had severe hypotonia, hyporeflexia, dysphagia with intermittent dependence on a nasogastric tube, moderate hearing impairment, and dysmorphic facial features. She was the only patient in this series born with a cleft palate, and she also had congenital bilateral hip dislocation with shallow acetabula and talipes equinovarus. Brain imaging showed moderate global brain atrophy. A similarly affected sib died without genetic testing. The proband of family F was born to consanguineous Turkish parents. Seizure onset was at 2 months of age, with focal-to-bilateral motor seizures with impaired awareness and hypsarrhythmia. At 3 years of age this child had severe delay in all milestones, could not sit or crawl, and had severe intellectual disability, high myopia, and severe hypotonia. Brain MRI was normal.

paragraphs.text: In 11 patients from 6 consanguineous families with DEE89, Chatron et al. (2020) identified homozygous mutations in the GAD1 gene. Sanger sequencing confirmed segregation with the disease. In family A, the 2 affected sibs were homozygous for a splice site mutation, c.1414-1G-C. In cDNA analysis this mutation abolished normal splicing: no normal mRNA product was detected, and there were 3 aberrant isoforms, with skipping of exon 15, retention of 76 bases of intron 14, or deletion of the first 7 bases of exon 15. The 2 affected sibs in family B were homozygous for an in-frame deletion, c.695_697delAGA, which deletes lys232 (K232del). The 2 affected sibs in family C were homozygous for a 5-bp deletion, c.812_816delTTAAG, which causes a frameshift (Val271AspfsTer9). Affected members of 2 families were homozygous for a nonsense mutation, c.1591C-T, which causes an arg531-to-ter substitution (R531X): the Iranian family D and the Turkish family E. The proband of family F was homozygous for a missense mutation, c.1525G-A, which causes a glu509-to-lys substitution (E509K).
